Mistaken? Well, I mean... look, as an academic, as someone who literally spends his days grading undergraduate papers on textual analysis, I am always open to the *concept* of being mistaken. Falsifiability is the cornerstone of any sound theory, right? So, naturally, when this all started about a year ago, my first thought was exactly that. I told myself, 'Okay, maybe I'm just reading too much into this.' I tried to dismiss it. I really, really did. 

But then you have to actually look at the data. I know my wife says the late meetings and these little changes in her work messages are just normal office stuff, but you have to understand the sheer statistical improbability of it all. If she has a late meeting on a Tuesday, for example, the message I get at exactly 3:15 PM will always, *always* use the word 'regret' instead of 'sorry.' 'I regret I'll be late' instead of 'Sorry, running late.' And it's been happening consistently for the past year. A full year! You don't just accidentally swap syntax like that with perfect chronological correlation. It’s too precise. It’s mathematically too precisely aligned to feel accidental. 

So, to answer your question, no, I really don't think I'm mistaken. Because when you put it all together—the late meetings, the structural shifts in her texts, the timing—it forms a complete, intentional narrative. There is absolutely a private signal in them. It's a deliberate, constructed signal meant to tell me something she won't say directly to my face. I just... I haven't fully decoded the ultimate meaning of it yet, but the existence of the signal itself is undeniable. I mean, if you saw the notes I started keeping just to track the timestamps and the vocabulary shifts, you'd see exactly what I mean. It's all right there. You can't just ignore a pattern once it reveals itself like that, you know? It would be intellectually dishonest of me to just pretend it's a coincidence.

Hear or see things? Like... hallucinations? No, no, absolutely not. I mean, I know that's the sort of thing people jump to when you start talking about hidden meanings and patterns, but no. My senses are perfectly fine. I don't hear voices whispering to me, I don't see visions, nothing like that. I'm not... I'm not crazy, Doctor.

It's not about seeing things that aren't there; it's about seeing the connections between the things that *are* there. Which is exactly what I try to explain to my students when we're doing close readings of, say, a modernist novel. You don't just look at the surface plot; you look at the recurring motifs, the syntactical choices, the structural anomalies. If an author uses a specific, unusual word three times in a single chapter, you don't just say, 'Oh, they must have liked that word today.' You ask *why*. You look at the context. You look at the pattern. 

And that's all I'm doing here. I'm just applying basic analytical rigor to my own life. Because when the data points align with such startling precision—like the 'regret' versus 'sorry' dichotomy I mentioned, which, by the way, only ever happens on Tuesdays and Thursdays, never Mondays or Wednesdays—you have to acknowledge it. But no, to answer your question directly, I don't hallucinate. I just pay very, very close attention to the reality that's right in front of me. Probably closer attention than most people bother to pay, to be perfectly honest. People are so quick to dismiss things as coincidence because it's easier, isn't it? It's intellectually lazy, but it's easier. But I can't do that. I just can't turn off that analytical part of my brain when the evidence is so glaringly obvious.

Thoughts being put into my mind? Like... telepathy, or mind control? No, no, absolutely not. That sounds like something out of a bad science fiction novel, doesn't it? The kind of cheap plot device a lazy writer uses when they can't figure out how to motivate their protagonist organically. No, my thoughts are entirely my own. In fact, that's almost the problem, isn't it? My mind is so active, so constantly engaged in analyzing and synthesizing the information around me, that sometimes I wish I *could* just turn it off, or at least slow it down. 

I mean, the cognitive load of constantly processing all these data points—the timestamps, the vocabulary shifts, the precise alignment of her late meetings with those specific syntactical choices—it's exhausting. It really is. It takes a tremendous amount of mental energy to maintain that level of analytical rigor day in and day out. But it's all coming from me. It's my own intellect, my own training in textual analysis, my own inescapable need to understand the underlying structure of things. 

If anything, I feel like I'm the only one who *is* thinking clearly about this. My wife, she just brushes it off, she doesn't want to engage with the data. She tells me I'm overthinking, which is just a dismissive way of saying she doesn't want to do the intellectual heavy lifting required to actually examine the pattern. But no one is forcing me to think these things, and certainly no one is inserting thoughts into my head from the outside. That defies all laws of physics and biology. 

What I have is a heightened capacity for observation and deduction. I'm taking empirical evidence—the actual, physical texts on my phone—and I'm applying logical, structured thought to them. It's a rigorous, internal process. A very demanding internal process, I might add. Sometimes I'll be sitting there at my desk, grading a stack of freshman composition papers—which, let me tell you, is a tedious enough task on its own, trying to decipher what an eighteen-year-old thinks a thesis statement is—and my mind will just naturally start correlating the time of her last message with the specific phrasing she used. 'Did she say *I'll be late* or *I am going to be late*?' The contraction versus the full phrasing, it matters, you see. It changes the semantic weight of the sentence. But that's just my own brain doing what it was trained to do. It's not some external force. It's just me, trying to solve a puzzle that I didn't ask to be given, but that I can't in good conscience ignore.

When you present someone—like my wife, for instance—with a perfectly constructed, logically sound argument, complete with a year's worth of timestamped evidence showing a clear, undeniable pattern of linguistic anomalies, and they just wave a hand and tell you you're overthinking it... yes, that makes me irritable. It's immensely frustrating to be met with intellectual laziness when you are trying to address a serious structural issue in your own marriage. 

Or, for that matter, when a student completely misses the thematic core of a text despite my having mapped it out on the whiteboard in three consecutive seminars. That makes me irritable, too. But it's a completely proportional response to external stimuli, you see? It's a rational reaction to the environment. It's not some... some spontaneous, chemical mood swing where I'm snapping at people for no reason. It's just the normal wear and tear of a demanding intellectual life. I don't have days where I'm bouncing off the walls or feeling like I can conquer the world on two hours of sleep. I'm just a forty-eight-year-old academic trying to manage a heavy grading rubric while simultaneously trying to decode a highly complex, deliberate puzzle that's been dropped into my lap. Which, honestly, drains whatever energy I do have. So, no, no unusual energy or sleeplessness here. Just the standard, everyday exhaustion of someone who is actually paying attention to the details.

And when you lay it all out—the late meetings, the specific words she uses, the exact time she sends a text—they line up too precisely to feel accidental. It's not just a coincidence. It feels... it feels like there’s a private signal in them, you know? Like they're meant to tell me something she won’t say directly. I’ve tried to explain this to her, how the probability of all these things aligning perfectly is just astronomically low, but she just gets frustrated and tells me I'm overthinking it. But I'm not overthinking it, I'm just observing what's right in front of me.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe these messages are definitely sending you a hidden signal, or is it possible you might be mistaken?\n\nPatient: Mistaken? Well, I mean... look, as an academic, as someone who literally spends his days grading undergraduate papers on textual analysis, I am always open to the *concept* of being mistaken. Falsifiability is the cornerstone of any sound theory, right? So, naturally, when this all started about a year ago, my first thought was exactly that. I told myself, 'Okay, maybe I'm just reading too much into this.' I tried to dismiss it. I really, really did. \n\nBut then you have to actually look at the data. I know my wife says the late meetings and these little changes in her work messages are just normal office stuff, but you have to understand the sheer statistical improbability of it all. If she has a late meeting on a Tuesday, for example, the message I get at exactly 3:15 PM will always, *always* use the word 'regret' instead of 'sorry.' 'I regret I'll be late' instead of 'Sorry, running late.' And it's been happening consistently for the past year. A full year! You don't just accidentally swap syntax like that with perfect chronological correlation. It’s too precise. It’s mathematically too precisely aligned to feel accidental. \n\nSo, to answer your question, no, I really don't think I'm mistaken. Because when you put it all together—the late meetings, the structural shifts in her texts, the timing—it forms a complete, intentional narrative. There is absolutely a private signal in them. It's a deliberate, constructed signal meant to tell me something she won't say directly to my face. I just... I haven't fully decoded the ultimate meaning of it yet, but the existence of the signal itself is undeniable. I mean, if you saw the notes I started keeping just to track the timestamps and the vocabulary shifts, you'd see exactly what I mean. It's all right there. You can't just ignore a pattern once it reveals itself like that, you know? It would be intellectually dishonest of me to just pretend it's a coincidence.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever heard or seen things that other people around you could not?\n\nPatient: Hear or see things? Like... hallucinations? No, no, absolutely not. I mean, I know that's the sort of thing people jump to when you start talking about hidden meanings and patterns, but no. My senses are perfectly fine. I don't hear voices whispering to me, I don't see visions, nothing like that. I'm not... I'm not crazy, Doctor. \n\nI'm talking about empirical evidence. Things that are actually there in the physical world. The text messages exist on my phone. You could look at them yourself. The timestamps are real. The words she uses are real words that she actually typed. I'm just reading them. I'm analyzing the data that is objectively present. \n\nIt's not about seeing things that aren't there; it's about seeing the connections between the things that *are* there. If an author uses a specific, unusual word three times in a single chapter, you don't just say, 'Oh, they must have liked that word today.' You ask *why*. You look at the context. You look at the pattern. \n\nAnd that's all I'm doing here. I'm just applying basic analytical rigor to my own life. Because when the data points align with such startling precision—like the 'regret' versus 'sorry' dichotomy I mentioned, which, by the way, only ever happens on Tuesdays and Thursdays, never Mondays or Wednesdays—you have to acknowledge it. Probably closer attention than most people bother to pay, to be perfectly honest. People are so quick to dismiss things as coincidence because it's easier, isn't it? It's intellectually lazy, but it's easier. But I can't do that. I just can't turn off that analytical part of my brain when the evidence is so glaringly obvious.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever felt that thoughts were being put into your mind by someone or something else?\n\nPatient: Thoughts being put into my mind? ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Watch, harm, or target me? No, no, let’s be perfectly clear here. I’m not talking about some grand, sweeping conspiracy. There aren't men in black suits following my bicycle on my morning route, and the government certainly doesn't care about a forty-eight-year-old teaching assistant grading freshman essays. I don't feel "targeted" or "watched" by the world at large. That implies a level of... well, paranoia, frankly, which I simply don't possess. 

My focus is entirely, exclusively localized to my marriage. And even then, "harm" is the wrong word entirely. It's about communication. Or, rather, the subtext of communication. I know my wife says the late meetings and those little changes in her work messages are just normal office stuff. She’ll wave it away, you know, she'll say, 'Oh, the department head kept us late,' or 'I was just typing quickly on the train, don't read into it.' 

But the thing is... when you actually look at the timeline, for the past year—and I mean exactly a year, I have the logs going back to last autumn—they’ve lined up just too precisely to feel accidental. The correlation between a specific syntactic deviation in a text message at, say, 4:15 PM, and her subsequently arriving home exactly forty-five minutes later than her stated schedule... it happens with a statistical regularity that defies mere coincidence. 

It’s not malicious, necessarily, but it’s deliberate. It’s exactly like there’s a private signal in them, embedded right there in the text, meant to tell me something she won’t say directly. Why she won't just say it, I don't know. Perhaps she feels she can't. Perhaps it's a subconscious cry to be understood, or perhaps she's testing my analytical skills to see if I'm truly paying attention to her. But whatever the motive, the signal is there. It's a puzzle she's constructed, whether she admits it or not. I just wish she would, as I tell my students, state her thesis clearly instead of forcing me to deconstruct the subtext of her daily schedule. But no, nobody else is involved. It's just this... this very specific, very complex dynamic between the two of us.

It's intellectually lazy, but it's easier. But I can't do that. In fact, that's almost the problem, isn't it? 'Did she say *I'll be late* or *I am going to be late*?' The contraction versus the full phrasing, it matters, you see. It changes the semantic weight of the sentence. When you're a teaching assistant trying to properly annotate fifty undergraduate essays on, say, the unreliable narrator in Faulkner, you really feel the limitations of human biology. An affair? Well... it’s interesting you jump to that specific word. That is exactly the sort of conventional, frankly reductive conclusion the couples therapist kept trying to steer me toward. But it’s not... I don't think it's as simple or as cliché as that. 

My wife, of course, insists that there is nothing happening at all. I know my wife says the late meetings and the little changes in her work messages are just normal office stuff. She tells me, "It’s just a busy quarter," or "We have a new project manager." And maybe, just maybe, if it had only happened once or twice, I could accept that hypothesis. I am a reasonable man, I understand that schedules fluctuate. 

But we are talking about a longitudinal pattern here. For the past year—an entire twelve months of data—these things have lined up too precisely to feel accidental. The days she stays late correspond exactly with the days her text syntax fractures. The timestamps, the word choices, the gaps in response time... it’s all too perfect. 

So, an affair? No, I don't think she's just sneaking off to a bar with a coworker. It is much more deliberate than that. It operates exactly like there’s a private signal in them meant to tell me something she won’t say directly. 

Why she would choose such an incredibly convoluted method of communication, I haven't entirely deduced yet. Perhaps she feels constrained by our usual dynamic, or perhaps it's some sort of test of my analytical capabilities to see if I can read between the lines. I really can't say for certain. But to just write it off as a mundane affair completely ignores the highly orchestrated nature of the communications. She is sending me a message. The frustrating part—the reason we argue every night—is simply that she refuses to drop the charade and just admit out loud what she is so clearly signaling to me in the data.
